register: Modern standard colloquial Bangladeshi Bengali (bn-BD), romanized. The course teaches apni — the respectful level of address — first and by default, because a learner's first hundred conversations are with strangers, shopkeepers, drivers, hosts and elders, and apni is what all of those ask for. Familiar tumi is not withheld as an advanced topic; it is given its own unit, where the contrast with apni is the lesson. Every item carries the level it belongs to, and the audit fails a lesson that mixes them by accident.
note: Romanization is the learner's reading interface and follows one spelling per word throughout: ache not achhe, geche not gechhe, dhonnobad not dhonyobad. Bengali script rides alongside every item for pronunciation and for anyone who wants it, and is never required to progress. Vocabulary ids are reused from content/learn-bengali.json wherever the same item is taught, so an existing learner's spaced-repetition memory and word bank survive the rebuild.
legal_note: Original content written for this app. No proprietary course material was copied.

question.prompt: So how would you ask for someone's name?
question.explanation: Add -r and the word becomes possessive: ami → amar (my), apni → apnar (your). It is the same -r both times, which is why amar naam is 'my name' and apnar naam is 'your name'.

question.prompt: Your friend's little brother asks your name. Which does he say?

question.prompt: Someone says 'kal ami ashbo'. When are they coming?

question.explanation: kal on its own means the day next to today — in either direction. The verb settles it: ashbo (I will come) makes it tomorrow, chilam (I was) makes it yesterday. Add goto for yesterday or agami for tomorrow when you need to be certain.

units.title: Visiting someone's home

vocabulary.context_en: Come in, sit down. — a host's words. You answer them; you do not say them.
Will you have something to eat? — you will hear this every single visit.

phrase_patterns.context_en: Could I have a little water?

I've enjoyed it very much. — the thing you say as you stand up.

question.prompt: You want to ask a host for water. Which is best?
question.explanation: chai says what you want; deben asks whether the other person will give it. Wrap it in ektu — 'a little' — and a request stops being a demand. This is the shape for hosts, shopkeepers and strangers alike.

question.explanation: The present puts na after the verb; the past does not. It fuses -ni onto the end instead: bujhechi becomes bujhini, gechilam becomes jaini. One ending, no separate word.

question.prompt: How would you say 'if you come, I'll be happy'?
question.explanation: Bengali can put jodi in front of the clause, or fuse -le onto the verb and drop jodi entirely. The -le version is shorter and far more common in speech, which is why it is worth having both.
